But should investors be confident in David Solomon?Mike Mayo is Wells Fargo's managing director and head of US large cap bank research. Mike, always great to get some time with you, especially in studio. So David Solomon saying things might be OK, things might be getting better. Should investors believe him?MIKE MAYO: Well, let's do the short-term, medium-term, and long-term. The short-term is this is a situation of sell on the rumor and buy on the news. We had been expecting, in our numbers, big write downs. You got big write downs.And you, as a firm, can't have $1.1 billion write downs every quarter as you pivot away from consumer, as you pivot away from an acquisition-- they did Green sky-- as they pivot away from these on balance sheet investments. And by the way, a lot of write downs for office specifically. So that's what's happening now. So the bad news is out there in the stocks up today. In fact, I actually increased my estimates because you've got some of the bad stuff out.In the medium-term, it waits to be seen how soon the capital markets come back. You've had lower for longer investment banking, you've had less volatility for trading. So in some ways, it's the worst of all worlds. But the backlog is up at Goldman Sachs versus last quarter, and the question is, how much of that backlog do you convert and monetize to revenues?Story continuesBut the long-term is what's really the big question here is. And Goldman Sachs is going back to the future by getting out of consumer, which I thought was stupid day one. You go back, any research, any time I've been on your show, like, why were they--- He's using a Goldman Sachs credit card. I mean, this is Amex. This is Amex land. Mastercard, Visa.- I don't even mean that, I mean, like, the Marcus lending. You're going to lead off to the mass consumer in the United States with a lending product? Sure. That doesn't create sticky relationships. And then they go ahead and do that with a savings account by charging-- that doesn't create sticky relationships.By the way, look at JP Morgan in London. They lead with a checking account where you interact several times a day. That builds sticky relationships. So I thought I was stupid. And the more it went on, it was even more ridiculous. So better late than never to pivot away from this.But now, they're going back to the future. Their legacy over the past 150 years has been serving large institutions. So 2/3 of the company is global banking and markets, where they get mid-teens returns, they have number one leadership in mergers for 20 years, this quarter, equities did great. So that part of the business, nobody has too much question about.Another 1/3 of the company is wealth and asset management. They are doing better in the wealth business but they have to get rid of some of these principal investments, which is a big drag from a regulatory perspective. And then there are extracurricular activities and consumer and some of these other things that they're getting rid of.So they get rid of the stuff that's extracurricular, they stay in their lane, they pivot and make themselves more balance sheet efficient and more operationally efficient. And then if and when these green shoots materialize, maybe, they get from a lowly core-- their ROE this quarter was 4%.This was the second worst quarter under David Solomon, excluding the pandemic. It was the worst quarter in over seven years for Goldman Sachs. So this is bad. You can't keep doing this. But their goal is to take it from the 4%, or 9% adjusted for the charges, up to 15% over the next two to three years.I don't have that. No one in consensus seems to have that. So no one's really believing David Solomon. So the bar is low. They're not trading too far above book value for a company that's grown book value faster than most banks.So I think this is an opportunity. The risk is that it just stays kind of dead money as other things go up. But this is a big pivot. This is a big day for Goldman Sachs. David Solomon is under pressure. So I think over the next year, we're going to have to see some signs that they're going toward that 15% return.- Mike, do you think Solomon is the right person for this job? Is he going to be able to steer Goldman in the right direction? Because there has been, like you just said, tremendous amount of pressure, not only from shareholders, but even within the firm, from partners who haven't been happy with the direction.MIKE MAYO: Well, look, like anyone else at Goldman Sachs, David Solomon has to earn the right to be in his job every day. I think from a strategic standpoint, this idea of focusing on two core businesses, pivoting out of the stuff that isn't so core is the right strategy.So really, it just comes down to execution. And can they execute on their plans. And that's why I'm here, that's why you're there, that's why all the eyes are there watching them quarter to quarter to quarter.So right now, David Solomon is still there. Actually, the stock price has outperformed since he's been there. Their capital markets activities grown much faster than the others since he's been there. They've exceeded book value faster. So on those metrics, it looks good. But I'm more concerned about the next three to five years.So, yes, David Solomon is the right person at the moment. But I'm still watching closely quarter by quarter by quarter.- Mike, I've followed your work, probably, for well over a decade, and there's been a theme during that decade. The leaders that are still operating this business, leading these companies as CEO, are still entrenched.Brian Moynihan, I talked to him yesterday, very much engaged. Doesn't sound like he's going anywhere anytime soon. Maybe Jamie Dimon finally bows out as CEO in the next two to three years. He's been teasing it for 10 years or whatever it is. Morgan Stanley seeing a change, and James Gorman in a year and a half. What has this current guard of CEOs meant to the financial services industry? And is the next crop of leaders, are they as good as these guys?MIKE MAYO: Well, these leaders were born out of the global financial crisis, which, as you recall, from 2008, 2009, was the biggest crisis since the Great Depression. And so they learned some pretty hard lessons. And so these are survivors from that crisis. And so what doesn't kill you makes you stronger.And that's certainly the case with Jamie Dimon, which bought Bear and WaMu during the global financial crisis. And then he comes back again and buys First Republic and acts as a leader. So look, I've had my spats with Jamie Dimon. And I just thought they were spending way too much a year and a half ago. And now they're showing incredible discipline.I mean, what company-- I mean, had an IPO on just now about beauty, right before oddity. I thought banks might be the-- that's the beauty, the banks are the beast, I guess. So today you have Beauty and the Beast.But, I mean, what company-- JP Morgan just guided for 10 billion higher in revenues between this quarter and last quarter, and guided for zero increase in expenses. That's amazing, after all the criticism I gave Jamie Dimon. So you're not going to find too many Jamie Dimons coming along.In terms of James Gorman, I said, in 2012-- I upgraded the stock-- I said, either stock price should go higher or he should be fired. And after that, James Gorman-- it was an inner day upgrade after they had a terrible fixed income quarter. James Gorman picks up the phone, calls me, I thought it was a joke at first. And the first reaction by him-- and he had his team, I had my team-- he said, so that wasn't very nice. And I said, well, I just think the stock should go higher. He goes, so do I. And let me tell you why I think it will.So this idea of not acting defensive-- you get red flags from people who act defensive. You see it on your show sometimes. But this was the opposite of acting defensive, being open-minded. So I think that sort of open mindedness-- you can have that, you might not have that. But when someone gets in the position, do they actually act that way?And Brian Moynihan, I also thought he should be fired. I went to a special shareholder meeting a decade ago and he proved me wrong. And frankly, I think I would have said the same thing a decade ago, I'm not sure he was ready to become CEO. But that's just grinded out quarter after quarter, year after year, build a better mousetrap.So I think they're all good in different ways. So there's definitely an opening for new leaders to emerge but they won't have been as battle tested as James Gorman, Brian Moynihan, or Jamie Dimon.- Point well taken. Mike Mayo, thanks for coming down on a very busy day for earnings. I know you have more to go. We appreciate it. It's a real treat.MIKE MAYO: Thanks for having me.- Thanks so much.]

column10: [(Adds bond price reaction, note conversion in paragraphs 6-8)July 21 (Reuters) - A unit of Swedish property group SBB will issue preference shares to an investment fund managed by Morgan Stanley to boost its liquidity and financial profile, SBB said on Friday.Following the transaction of shares worth 2.36 billion Swedish crowns ($228 million), Morgan Stanley Real Estate Investing will hold a minority stake in SBB Residential Property, the company said in a statement.The unit, which currently comprises rent-regulated residential properties in Sweden with a fair value of about 6.2 billion crowns as of June 30, 2023, will be controlled and operated by SBB.The preference shares have no maturity date and no payment obligation, and rely on the return of capital on an exit or by SBB redeeming the shares.SBB is scrambling to salvage its finances after recently seeing its credit rating downgraded to junk. Its shares have lost over 90% of their value since peaking in 2021.Some of SBB's bonds were up between 1 and 3 crown cents on Friday, according to Tradeweb data, as investors welcomed the news of the fundraising.On Friday, the company also said in a separate statement that holders of a mandatory convertible note worth 10 million crowns had converted them into B-shares.The notes were the remaining part of an original 2.75 billion crowns subordinated mandatory convertible note issued in 2021 and due this year. Following the conversion, no convertible note remains outstanding.High debt, rising interest rates and a wilting economy have produced a toxic cocktail for Sweden's commercial property companies, with many such as SBB seeing their credit status cut to junk.($1 = 10.3449 Swedish crowns) (Reporting by Shivani Tanna and Mrinmay Dey in Bengaluru, Marie Mannes in Stockholm and Chiara Elisei in London; Editing by Muralikumar Anantharaman and Christian Schmollinger)]

column4: Wall Street says the worst is over for Wall Street
column10: [Wall Street is making the case that the the worst is over for Wall Street. So far investors agree.Top bank executives spent much of this past week pointing to "green shoots" in dealmaking or trading despite in most cases logging another disappointing quarter.Morgan Stanley (MS) CFO Sharon Yeshaya said that "sentiment and activity improved towards the end of the quarter, evidenced by green shoots that emerged across our businesses."Citigroup (C) CFO Mark Mason said "we are seeing green shoots" in the issuance of debt "as clients start to have a greater conviction" about the direction of interest rates.Goldman Sachs (GS) CEO David Solomon said Wednesday that the month of June "was certainly better" than the earlier part of the quarter and that he has noticed more "risk-on sentiment" in July.David M. Solomon, CEO of Goldman Sachs. (REUTERS/Mike Blake) (Mike Blake / reuters)"It definitely feels better over the course of the last six to eight weeks than it felt earlier in the year."That's certainly what investors wanted to hear. Stocks of most big banks rose this past week. Morgan Stanley's stock was up more than 6% on Tuesday after its results were released. Goldman's stock even rose more than 1% Wednesday despite reporting that profits fell by 58%, more than expected.Yet the performance of Wall Street's core businesses were certainly nothing to celebrate across most banks. Trading revenue fell by 22% at Morgan Stanley, 14% at Goldman, 13% at Citigroup, and 10% at JPMorgan Chase. Only Bank of America (BAC) had trading revenue rise, by 7%.The drops were not as much as analysts expected at all but one firm, Morgan Stanley.Investment banking revenues were down by 24% at Citi, 20% at Goldman, and 6% at JPMorgan. They were flat at Morgan Stanley and up 1.6% at Bank of America.The drops at Goldman and Citigroup were worse than expected. For the others, the results beat estimates.'We feel good about where we are'The global slowdown in dealmaking began last year after a boom in 2021, causing firms across Wall Street to slash bonuses and staff. It continued in 2023 as worldwide investment banking revenues for the second quarter fell 52% from a year ago, according to Dealogic.Story continuesGoldman, Morgan Stanley, and Citigroup were among the firms on Wall Street that have made or announced cuts of roughly 20,000 jobs since the end of 2022, resulting in hundreds of millions in severance costs.Goldman spent $260 million through the first half of the year and Citigroup spent $450 million. Morgan Stanley's severance costs were $308 million in the second quarter.Some executives hinted this week that the headcount reductions were likely over."I'm glad we were early in January to work on head count sizing," Solomon said, referring to a decision that month to lay off more than 3,000 workers. But now, "we feel good about where we are."'We will see'Solomon said he is noticing activity picking up in a few spots, citing equity capital markets and mergers and acquisitions."When I go back and I look historically at other periods where the macro environment has created sharp drops in investment banking activity, they tend to last for a year or so and then they start to improve," the CEO said. "And so I think we're starting to see that here. It definitely feels better."Goldman, he added, doesn't have to go back to the boom period of 2021 to see "material uplift."At Morgan Stanley, Yeshaya said the firm's backlog of deals is on the rise and M&A activity is picking up in energy and financials.Mason, at Citigoup, cited a "healthy" M&A pipeline "which we would expect to unlock as the sentiment continues to improve." Still the company has "more work to do" on equity capital markets and M&A.His boss, CEO Jane Fraser, also sounded a cautious note. In a release she said that "the long-awaited rebound in investment banking has yet to materialize."Then she told analysts "corporates are pretty cautious," citing the prospect of another Federal Reserve interest rate hike, tensions with China, and concerns about limited economic growth.Citigroup CEO Jane Fraser. (AP Photo/Andrew Harnik) (ASSOCIATED PRESS)"I think clients have been trying to understand and get their arms around both the macro and the market outlook for a while," she added. "I think they now seem to accept the current environment is the new normal and are beginning to position themselves globally."JPMorgan CFO Jeremy Barnum said investment banking was better than expected in June, but cautioned analysts on Friday that it was "too early" to label it a trend."We will see," he said. For overall capital markets "July should be a good indicator for the remainder of the year."Click here for the latest stock market news and in-depth analysis, including events that move stocksRead the latest financial and business news from Yahoo Finance]

column4: Wall Street says the worst is over for Wall Street
column10: [Wall Street is making the case that the the worst is over for Wall Street. So far investors agree.Top bank executives spent much of this past week pointing to "green shoots" in dealmaking or trading despite in most cases logging another disappointing quarter.Morgan Stanley (MS) CFO Sharon Yeshaya said that "sentiment and activity improved towards the end of the quarter, evidenced by green shoots that emerged across our businesses."Citigroup (C) CFO Mark Mason said "we are seeing green shoots" in the issuance of debt "as clients start to have a greater conviction" about the direction of interest rates.Goldman Sachs (GS) CEO David Solomon said Wednesday that the month of June "was certainly better" than the earlier part of the quarter and that he has noticed more "risk-on sentiment" in July.David M. Solomon, CEO of Goldman Sachs. (REUTERS/Mike Blake) (Mike Blake / reuters)"It definitely feels better over the course of the last six to eight weeks than it felt earlier in the year."That's certainly what investors wanted to hear. Stocks of most big banks rose this past week. Morgan Stanley's stock was up more than 6% on Tuesday after its results were released. Goldman's stock even rose more than 1% Wednesday despite reporting that profits fell by 58%, more than expected.Yet the performance of Wall Street's core businesses were certainly nothing to celebrate across most banks. Trading revenue fell by 22% at Morgan Stanley, 14% at Goldman, 13% at Citigroup, and 10% at JPMorgan Chase. Only Bank of America (BAC) had trading revenue rise, by 7%.The drops were not as much as analysts expected at all but one firm, Morgan Stanley.Investment banking revenues were down by 24% at Citi, 20% at Goldman, and 6% at JPMorgan. They were flat at Morgan Stanley and up 1.6% at Bank of America.The drops at Goldman and Citigroup were worse than expected. For the others, the results beat estimates.'We feel good about where we are'The global slowdown in dealmaking began last year after a boom in 2021, causing firms across Wall Street to slash bonuses and staff. It continued in 2023 as worldwide investment banking revenues for the second quarter fell 52% from a year ago, according to Dealogic.Story continuesGoldman, Morgan Stanley, and Citigroup were among the firms on Wall Street that have made or announced cuts of roughly 20,000 jobs since the end of 2022, resulting in hundreds of millions in severance costs.Goldman spent $260 million through the first half of the year and Citigroup spent $450 million. Morgan Stanley's severance costs were $308 million in the second quarter.Some executives hinted this week that the headcount reductions were likely over."I'm glad we were early in January to work on head count sizing," Solomon said, referring to a decision that month to lay off more than 3,000 workers. But now, "we feel good about where we are."'We will see'Solomon said he is noticing activity picking up in a few spots, citing equity capital markets and mergers and acquisitions."When I go back and I look historically at other periods where the macro environment has created sharp drops in investment banking activity, they tend to last for a year or so and then they start to improve," the CEO said. "And so I think we're starting to see that here. It definitely feels better."Goldman, he added, doesn't have to go back to the boom period of 2021 to see "material uplift."At Morgan Stanley, Yeshaya said the firm's backlog of deals is on the rise and M&A activity is picking up in energy and financials.Mason, at Citigoup, cited a "healthy" M&A pipeline "which we would expect to unlock as the sentiment continues to improve." Still the company has "more work to do" on equity capital markets and M&A.His boss, CEO Jane Fraser, also sounded a cautious note. In a release she said that "the long-awaited rebound in investment banking has yet to materialize."Then she told analysts "corporates are pretty cautious," citing the prospect of another Federal Reserve interest rate hike, tensions with China, and concerns about limited economic growth.Citigroup CEO Jane Fraser. (AP Photo/Andrew Harnik) (ASSOCIATED PRESS)"I think clients have been trying to understand and get their arms around both the macro and the market outlook for a while," she added. "I think they now seem to accept the current environment is the new normal and are beginning to position themselves globally."JPMorgan CFO Jeremy Barnum said investment banking was better than expected in June, but cautioned analysts on Friday that it was "too early" to label it a trend."We will see," he said. For overall capital markets "July should be a good indicator for the remainder of the year."Click here for the latest stock market news and in-depth analysis, including events that move stocksRead the latest financial and business news from Yahoo Finance]

column10: [Morgan Stanley (NYSE:MS) has announced that it will be increasing its dividend from last year's comparable payment on the 15th of August to $0.85. This takes the dividend yield to 3.6%, which shareholders will be pleased with. Check out our latest analysis for Morgan Stanley Morgan Stanley's Earnings Easily Cover The DistributionsWe like to see robust dividend yields, but that doesn't matter if the payment isn't sustainable. Based on the last payment, Morgan Stanley's earnings were much higher than the dividend, but it wasn't converting those earnings into cash flow. No cash flows could definitely make returning cash to shareholders difficult, or at least mean the balance sheet will come under pressure.Looking forward, earnings per share is forecast to rise by 36.7% over the next year. Assuming the dividend continues along recent trends, we think the payout ratio could be 50% by next year, which is in a pretty sustainable range.historic-dividendMorgan Stanley Has A Solid Track RecordThe company has a sustained record of paying dividends with very little fluctuation. The dividend has gone from an annual total of $0.20 in 2013 to the most recent total annual payment of $3.40. This works out to be a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of approximately 33% a year over that time. So, dividends have been growing pretty quickly, and even more impressively, they haven't experienced any notable falls during this period.We Could See Morgan Stanley's Dividend GrowingSome investors will be chomping at the bit to buy some of the company's stock based on its dividend history. Morgan Stanley has seen EPS rising for the last five years, at 7.4% per annum. While on an earnings basis, this company looks appealing as an income stock, the cash payout ratio still makes us cautious.In SummaryIn summary, while it's always good to see the dividend being raised, we don't think Morgan Stanley's payments are rock solid. column4: Embattled SBB Narrows Financing Gap With $228 Million Share Sale
UPDATE 2-Swedish landlord SBB raising $228 mln capital from Morgan Stanley fund
column10: [(Adds bond price reaction, note conversion in paragraphs 6-8)July 21 (Reuters) - A unit of Swedish property group SBB will issue preference shares to an investment fund managed by Morgan Stanley to boost its liquidity and financial profile, SBB said on Friday.Following the transaction of shares worth 2.36 billion Swedish crowns ($228 million), Morgan Stanley Real Estate Investing will hold a minority stake in SBB Residential Property, the company said in a statement.The unit, which currently comprises rent-regulated residential properties in Sweden with a fair value of about 6.2 billion crowns as of June 30, 2023, will be controlled and operated by SBB.The preference shares have no maturity date and no payment obligation, and rely on the return of capital on an exit or by SBB redeeming the shares.SBB is scrambling to salvage its finances after recently seeing its credit rating downgraded to junk. Its shares have lost over 90% of their value since peaking in 2021.Some of SBB's bonds were up between 1 and 3 crown cents on Friday, according to Tradeweb data, as investors welcomed the news of the fundraising.On Friday, the company also said in a separate statement that holders of a mandatory convertible note worth 10 million crowns had converted them into B-shares.The notes were the remaining part of an original 2.75 billion crowns subordinated mandatory convertible note issued in 2021 and due this year. Following the conversion, no convertible note remains outstanding.High debt, rising interest rates and a wilting economy have produced a toxic cocktail for Sweden's commercial property companies, with many such as SBB seeing their credit status cut to junk.($1 = 10.3449 Swedish crowns) (Reporting by Shivani Tanna and Mrinmay Dey in Bengaluru, Marie Mannes in Stockholm and Chiara Elisei in London; Editing by Muralikumar Anantharaman and Christian Schmollinger)]

MOVES-Morgan Stanley hires Kagan from Citi for structured M&A -sources
column10: [By Anirban SenNEW YORK, July 24 (Reuters) - Morgan Stanley has hired Michael Kagan from Citigroup Inc to drive the bank's efforts on structured mergers and acquisitions (M&A), including spin-offs and separation deals, people familiar with the matter said on Monday.Kagan was Citigroup's North America head of shareholder advisory and structured solutions. The sources requested anonymity because the matter is confidential.Morgan Stanley and Citigroup declined to comment.Before joining Citi, Kagan worked on structuring deals at Goldman Sachs Group Inc for nearly a decade. He started his career as a tax associate at law firm Cleary Gottlieb Steen & Hamilton LLP.A number of Wall Street banks have investment banking teams that work on so-called structured deals, which include corporate restructuring transactions such as corporate carveouts and spin-outs.At Goldman Sachs, for instance, David Dubner leads its M&A structuring unit, while former Goldman banker Joe Todd spearheads Evercore Inc's spin-off business.Kagan's hiring comes as more companies mull ways to shed non-core assets amid concerns about an economic slowdown. Just in 2022, there were 30 separation deals globally, representing about 17% of all the spin-off transactions that were unveiled during the last decade, according to data compiled by Goldman Sachs and EY.Roughly half of such deals from the 2018-to-2022 period were worth over $5 billion, compared with a third from the 2012 to 2017 period that met that threshold, according to the Goldman-EY study.Morgan Stanley has also made other high-profile hires of late to boost its investment banking franchise. It hired Marco Caggiano, who previously served as JPMorgan Chase & Co's North America head of M&A, following the departure of veteran investment banker Rob Kindler, who is joining law firm Paul, Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton & Garrison LLP. (Reporting by Anirban Sen in New York Editing by Marguerita Choy)]

column4: 5 Stocks With Recent Dividend Hike to Watch Ahead of July FOMC
column10: [The Fed paused the current interest rate hike cycle in its June FOMC meeting after 10 consecutive increases. However, Fed Chairman Jerome Powell warned that more rate hikes are expected this year. The “dot plot” of the June FOMC showed that the majority of Fed officials expected two more rate hike of 25 basis points each this year.The inflation rate stayed elevated well above the central bank’s 2% target rate despite a stiff fall from its 40-year peak in June 2022. The major concern for the Fed is a resilient U.S. labor market. Although job additions in June were lower than expectations, it was in line with the historical average. Moreover, the wage rate remained sticky downward.Market participants are expecting the Fed to hike the benchmark interest rate again in the July FOMC meeting. At present, the CME FedWatch indicates almost a 100% probability that the Fed will raise the benchmark lending rate by 25 basis points to a range of 5.25-5.5% in July. No rate cut is expected this year. column4: Embattled SBB Narrows Financing Gap With $228 Million Share Sale
UPDATE 2-Swedish landlord SBB raising $228 mln capital from Morgan Stanley fund
column10: [(Adds bond price reaction, note conversion in paragraphs 6-8)July 21 (Reuters) - A unit of Swedish property group SBB will issue preference shares to an investment fund managed by Morgan Stanley to boost its liquidity and financial profile, SBB said on Friday.Following the transaction of shares worth 2.36 billion Swedish crowns ($228 million), Morgan Stanley Real Estate Investing will hold a minority stake in SBB Residential Property, the company said in a statement.The unit, which currently comprises rent-regulated residential properties in Sweden with a fair value of about 6.2 billion crowns as of June 30, 2023, will be controlled and operated by SBB.The preference shares have no maturity date and no payment obligation, and rely on the return of capital on an exit or by SBB redeeming the shares.SBB is scrambling to salvage its finances after recently seeing its credit rating downgraded to junk. Its shares have lost over 90% of their value since peaking in 2021.Some of SBB's bonds were up between 1 and 3 crown cents on Friday, according to Tradeweb data, as investors welcomed the news of the fundraising.On Friday, the company also said in a separate statement that holders of a mandatory convertible note worth 10 million crowns had converted them into B-shares.The notes were the remaining part of an original 2.75 billion crowns subordinated mandatory convertible note issued in 2021 and due this year. Following the conversion, no convertible note remains outstanding.High debt, rising interest rates and a wilting economy have produced a toxic cocktail for Sweden's commercial property companies, with many such as SBB seeing their credit status cut to junk.($1 = 10.3449 Swedish crowns) (Reporting by Shivani Tanna and Mrinmay Dey in Bengaluru, Marie Mannes in Stockholm and Chiara Elisei in London; Editing by Muralikumar Anantharaman and Christian Schmollinger)]

column4: Fed set to propose new banking capital requirements, 'Basel III endgame'
column10: [Fed officials are set to unveil an overhaul of banking capital requirements, known as the "Basel III endgame," this week. American Banker Staff Writer Kyle Campbell sits down with Yahoo Finance Live to explain the ways in which these guidelines will mitigate risk differently for various forms of credit lending. Campbell describes how these new guidelines will impact certain larger, institutional banks, while examining the exposure regional banks may have to commercial real estate.Video Transcript- All right. On Thursday, just one day after the FOMC's latest interest rate decision, Federal Reserve will unveil a proposal for new bank capital requirements. The proposed rule would also lower the threshold for qualifying banks, meaning smaller institutions will face a new host of demands previously avoided.Fed vice chair for supervision, Michael Barr, outlined a sweeping plan to overhaul bank oversight requirements earlier this month. The proposal, set to come out Thursday, will offer more specifics on just how significant those changes could be.Joining us now with the latest is Kyle Campbell, staff writer at American Banker. Kyle, good to see you here. I talked to Brian Moynihan, CEO of Bank of America, about this. He really took a-- I would say, a hard line view of this. This could really be impactful to the economy. What have you been hearing from sources?KYLE CAMPBELL: Yeah, I mean, that's the big concern, right. Banks have been looking forward to this proposal for a long time now. Since 2017 is when the Basel III, they call it endgame, was first finalized, sort of, internationally, and now we're implementing that.Where this is-- what we're going to see on Thursday is just how that's going to impact the economy because we're going to find out which particular activities are going to be given which sort of risk weights under the new framework. So if, let's say, auto lending comes with a much heavier capital penalty, than a lot of banks are sort of forecasting with their internal models currently. It's going to make that type of financing more expensive, essentially.Story continuesAnd there is a view that as capital overall increases, it's just going to have a broader, sort of, tightening impact on the availability of credit broadly in the economy.- Is it really? Or is it just that their margins are going to get smaller? Or both, right?KYLE CAMPBELL: I think it's probably a bit of both but that's a great question. And certainly, consumer advocates are saying, well, look, the way that capital is raised is it's just hurting the bottom line for executives. You just have to retained earnings and you lose that sort of ROE, return on equity, that is what sort of fuels bank profits.So it's certainly going to result in less profitability, at least for some period of time. And again, how that actually impacts the availability of credit to the average person is going to really, I think-- I don't think it's particularly useful to try to forecast the overall picture, but you can get a good sense of how individual banks are going to be impacted by this once we see the specifics on Thursday.- For those banks, let's say a Wells Fargo, that have been struggling for some time, what does this mean for the struggling banks like a Wells Fargo?KYLE CAMPBELL: Wells Fargo, it'll be interesting. I mean, obviously if-- I mean, they've started to sort of move away from mortgages, which is one area where there's going to be a lot of focus. What happens to mortgages. You know, how does it get treated under the capital rules.I mean-- I think that where it's going to be more impactful than at Wells Fargo-- I mean, certainly they're going to be hit to some degree. But I think it's really going to be most impactful on the sort of mid-size banks, if you will. The ones that were in that sort of 100 billion to 250 billion asset range, that are now going to be facing these capital-- these sort of risk capital requirements for the first time.I think the large banks sort of know how to deal with these sort of requirements. And I don't think that a Wells Fargo is going to be as impacted, on a relative basis, as some of the smaller banks.- Let's turn to another issue that the market's been paying a lot of attention to, and that's commercial real estate and the risks associated with commercial real estate. In these earnings reports that we've gotten from banks, several of them announced steps to anticipate losses. To put aside money for losses, potential losses in commercial real estate.Wells Fargo, for example, boosted its allowance for credit losses. So where are we in that sort of situation?KYLE CAMPBELL: Yeah, that's a great question. And certainly, regulators are very focused on commercial real estate, giving some strong warnings to banks to do things like set aside losses and sort of avoid getting new exposures where you can avoid it.And that actually kind of compounds the issue because a lot of these-- I mean, certainly with offices, we know, the ones that are vacant, not getting people in, and that's sort of a whole issue unto itself. But there are some assets where they're kind of performing relatively well but they're going to need some kind of a recapitalization in order to remain viable and not end up as a foreclosure. And in order to do that, you need banks to sort come to the table.So I think what we're going to be looking for is who's going to move first. Are we going to see some of these sort of big capital equity investors, private equity funds, start to come in and say, hey, we're going to move in in a higher equity basis? Or are we going to see some banks say, hey, actually, we're going to be willing to back some of these recap-type strategies through lending?- Is this a potentially destabilizing event for the banking sector?KYLE CAMPBELL: I wouldn't think so.- I'm trying to compare it to what happened earlier this year.KYLE CAMPBELL: Right. Yeah. I mean, I think you're going to see some serious stress. And I wouldn't be surprised if at specific banks, you see some possible failures. I mean, you don't want to throw that term around too lightly. But yeah, it's possible that some banks could either have to be sold or go through some sort of an M&A activity to sort of right the ship here.I wouldn't expect it to get to a level where we're needing to see serious intervention by the government because they're sort of very well aware of what's going on in real time. But these things can snowball pretty quickly. So yeah, it could be something to watch for sure.- Yeah, most definitely. Kyle, thanks for coming in. Good to see you. Kyle Campbell, staff writer at American Banker, covering some various areas of risks for us.]

MOVES-Morgan Stanley hires Kagan from Citi for structured M&A -sources
column10: [By Anirban SenNEW YORK, July 24 (Reuters) - Morgan Stanley has hired Michael Kagan from Citigroup Inc to drive the bank's efforts on structured mergers and acquisitions (M&A), including spin-offs and separation deals, people familiar with the matter said on Monday.Kagan was Citigroup's North America head of shareholder advisory and structured solutions. The sources requested anonymity because the matter is confidential.Morgan Stanley and Citigroup declined to comment.Before joining Citi, Kagan worked on structuring deals at Goldman Sachs Group Inc for nearly a decade. He started his career as a tax associate at law firm Cleary Gottlieb Steen & Hamilton LLP.A number of Wall Street banks have investment banking teams that work on so-called structured deals, which include corporate restructuring transactions such as corporate carveouts and spin-outs.At Goldman Sachs, for instance, David Dubner leads its M&A structuring unit, while former Goldman banker Joe Todd spearheads Evercore Inc's spin-off business.Kagan's hiring comes as more companies mull ways to shed non-core assets amid concerns about an economic slowdown. Just in 2022, there were 30 separation deals globally, representing about 17% of all the spin-off transactions that were unveiled during the last decade, according to data compiled by Goldman Sachs and EY.Roughly half of such deals from the 2018-to-2022 period were worth over $5 billion, compared with a third from the 2012 to 2017 period that met that threshold, according to the Goldman-EY study.Morgan Stanley has also made other high-profile hires of late to boost its investment banking franchise. It hired Marco Caggiano, who previously served as JPMorgan Chase & Co's North America head of M&A, following the departure of veteran investment banker Rob Kindler, who is joining law firm Paul, Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton & Garrison LLP. (Reporting by Anirban Sen in New York Editing by Marguerita Choy)]

Check out our latest analysis for Morgan Stanley Morgan Stanley's Earnings Easily Cover The DistributionsWe like to see robust dividend yields, but that doesn't matter if the payment isn't sustainable. Based on the last payment, Morgan Stanley's earnings were much higher than the dividend, but it wasn't converting those earnings into cash flow. No cash flows could definitely make returning cash to shareholders difficult, or at least mean the balance sheet will come under pressure.Looking forward, earnings per share is forecast to rise by 36.7% over the next year. Assuming the dividend continues along recent trends, we think the payout ratio could be 50% by next year, which is in a pretty sustainable range.historic-dividendMorgan Stanley Has A Solid Track RecordThe company has a sustained record of paying dividends with very little fluctuation. The dividend has gone from an annual total of $0.20 in 2013 to the most recent total annual payment of $3.40. This works out to be a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of approximately 33% a year over that time. So, dividends have been growing pretty quickly, and even more impressively, they haven't experienced any notable falls during this period.We Could See Morgan Stanley's Dividend GrowingSome investors will be chomping at the bit to buy some of the company's stock based on its dividend history. Morgan Stanley has seen EPS rising for the last five years, at 7.4% per annum. While on an earnings basis, this company looks appealing as an income stock, the cash payout ratio still makes us cautious.In SummaryIn summary, while it's always good to see the dividend being raised, we don't think Morgan Stanley's payments are rock solid. With cash flows lacking, it is difficult to see how the company can sustain a dividend payment. column4: Embattled SBB Narrows Financing Gap With $228 Million Share Sale
UPDATE 2-Swedish landlord SBB raising $228 mln capital from Morgan Stanley fund
column10: [(Adds bond price reaction, note conversion in paragraphs 6-8)July 21 (Reuters) - A unit of Swedish property group SBB will issue preference shares to an investment fund managed by Morgan Stanley to boost its liquidity and financial profile, SBB said on Friday.Following the transaction of shares worth 2.36 billion Swedish crowns ($228 million), Morgan Stanley Real Estate Investing will hold a minority stake in SBB Residential Property, the company said in a statement.The unit, which currently comprises rent-regulated residential properties in Sweden with a fair value of about 6.2 billion crowns as of June 30, 2023, will be controlled and operated by SBB.The preference shares have no maturity date and no payment obligation, and rely on the return of capital on an exit or by SBB redeeming the shares.SBB is scrambling to salvage its finances after recently seeing its credit rating downgraded to junk. Its shares have lost over 90% of their value since peaking in 2021.Some of SBB's bonds were up between 1 and 3 crown cents on Friday, according to Tradeweb data, as investors welcomed the news of the fundraising.On Friday, the company also said in a separate statement that holders of a mandatory convertible note worth 10 million crowns had converted them into B-shares.The notes were the remaining part of an original 2.75 billion crowns subordinated mandatory convertible note issued in 2021 and due this year. Following the conversion, no convertible note remains outstanding.High debt, rising interest rates and a wilting economy have produced a toxic cocktail for Sweden's commercial property companies, with many such as SBB seeing their credit status cut to junk.($1 = 10.3449 Swedish crowns) (Reporting by Shivani Tanna and Mrinmay Dey in Bengaluru, Marie Mannes in Stockholm and Chiara Elisei in London; Editing by Muralikumar Anantharaman and Christian Schmollinger)]

UPDATE 1-Evercore hires veteran investment banker Bergstein from Morgan Stanley -sources
column10: [(Updates with Evercore and PJT declining to comment in last paragraph)By David Carnevali and Mike StoneNEW YORK, July 26 (Reuters) - Evercore has hired veteran Morgan Stanley banker Seth Bergstein as a senior managing director to drive dealmaking in the global services sector, people familiar with the matter said on Wednesday.Bergstein, who served as head of Morgan Stanley's global services group for about two decades, held the title of vice chairman of investment banking prior to his departure from the bank.He started his career at the Wall Street bank in the late 1980s as a financial analyst and briefly joined Goldman Sachs in 1991 before returning to Morgan Stanley, according to his LinkedIn profile.Bergstein's exit is the latest in a flurry of executive moves from large banks to boutique firms and comes at a time of a slowdown in mergers and acquisitions (M&A) activity that has forced Wall Street's biggest banks to cut thousands of investment banking jobs.Global M&A volumes for the first half of 2023 fell 39% to $1.38 trillion, according to data from Dealogic.In recent months, Evercore has hired more than half a dozen senior bankers from bigger investment banking rivals such as Goldman Sachs to boost its coverage in sectors such as technology and industrials.In June, Evercore hired veteran technology banker Tammy Kiely and top aerospace & defense banker Michael Tarulli from Goldman. Earlier this month, it recruited Neil Wolitzer, a partner in real estate investment banking at Goldman, one of the sources said.Meanwhile, PJT Partners Inc, the boutique investment bank led by Paul Taubman, has hired Brendan Panda, a prominent aerospace & defense dealmaker, from Evercore, the sources said. Panda worked on several notable transactions during his time at Evercore, including Aerojet Rocketdyne's $4.7 billion sale to L3Harris.Panda will join PJT as a partner focused on the aerospace & defense sector, the sources said.Evercore, PJT Partners and Morgan Stanley declined to comment. (Reporting by David Carnevali in New York; Editing by Sonali Paul)]

Fed set to propose new banking capital requirements, 'Basel III endgame'
column10: [Fed officials are set to unveil an overhaul of banking capital requirements, known as the "Basel III endgame," this week. American Banker Staff Writer Kyle Campbell sits down with Yahoo Finance Live to explain the ways in which these guidelines will mitigate risk differently for various forms of credit lending. Campbell describes how these new guidelines will impact certain larger, institutional banks, while examining the exposure regional banks may have to commercial real estate.Video Transcript- All right. On Thursday, just one day after the FOMC's latest interest rate decision, Federal Reserve will unveil a proposal for new bank capital requirements. The proposed rule would also lower the threshold for qualifying banks, meaning smaller institutions will face a new host of demands previously avoided.Fed vice chair for supervision, Michael Barr, outlined a sweeping plan to overhaul bank oversight requirements earlier this month. The proposal, set to come out Thursday, will offer more specifics on just how significant those changes could be.Joining us now with the latest is Kyle Campbell, staff writer at American Banker. Kyle, good to see you here. I talked to Brian Moynihan, CEO of Bank of America, about this. He really took a-- I would say, a hard line view of this. This could really be impactful to the economy. What have you been hearing from sources?KYLE CAMPBELL: Yeah, I mean, that's the big concern, right. Banks have been looking forward to this proposal for a long time now. Since 2017 is when the Basel III, they call it endgame, was first finalized, sort of, internationally, and now we're implementing that.Where this is-- what we're going to see on Thursday is just how that's going to impact the economy because we're going to find out which particular activities are going to be given which sort of risk weights under the new framework. So if, let's say, auto lending comes with a much heavier capital penalty, than a lot of banks are sort of forecasting with their internal models currently. It's going to make that type of financing more expensive, essentially.Story continuesAnd there is a view that as capital overall increases, it's just going to have a broader, sort of, tightening impact on the availability of credit broadly in the economy.- Is it really? Or is it just that their margins are going to get smaller? Or both, right?KYLE CAMPBELL: I think it's probably a bit of both but that's a great question. And certainly, consumer advocates are saying, well, look, the way that capital is raised is it's just hurting the bottom line for executives. You just have to retained earnings and you lose that sort of ROE, return on equity, that is what sort of fuels bank profits.So it's certainly going to result in less profitability, at least for some period of time. And again, how that actually impacts the availability of credit to the average person is going to really, I think-- I don't think it's particularly useful to try to forecast the overall picture, but you can get a good sense of how individual banks are going to be impacted by this once we see the specifics on Thursday.- For those banks, let's say a Wells Fargo, that have been struggling for some time, what does this mean for the struggling banks like a Wells Fargo?KYLE CAMPBELL: Wells Fargo, it'll be interesting. I mean, obviously if-- I mean, they've started to sort of move away from mortgages, which is one area where there's going to be a lot of focus. What happens to mortgages. You know, how does it get treated under the capital rules.I mean-- I think that where it's going to be more impactful than at Wells Fargo-- I mean, certainly they're going to be hit to some degree. But I think it's really going to be most impactful on the sort of mid-size banks, if you will. The ones that were in that sort of 100 billion to 250 billion asset range, that are now going to be facing these capital-- these sort of risk capital requirements for the first time.I think the large banks sort of know how to deal with these sort of requirements. And I don't think that a Wells Fargo is going to be as impacted, on a relative basis, as some of the smaller banks.- Let's turn to another issue that the market's been paying a lot of attention to, and that's commercial real estate and the risks associated with commercial real estate. In these earnings reports that we've gotten from banks, several of them announced steps to anticipate losses. To put aside money for losses, potential losses in commercial real estate.Wells Fargo, for example, boosted its allowance for credit losses. So where are we in that sort of situation?KYLE CAMPBELL: Yeah, that's a great question. And certainly, regulators are very focused on commercial real estate, giving some strong warnings to banks to do things like set aside losses and sort of avoid getting new exposures where you can avoid it.And that actually kind of compounds the issue because a lot of these-- I mean, certainly with offices, we know, the ones that are vacant, not getting people in, and that's sort of a whole issue unto itself. But there are some assets where they're kind of performing relatively well but they're going to need some kind of a recapitalization in order to remain viable and not end up as a foreclosure. And in order to do that, you need banks to sort come to the table.So I think what we're going to be looking for is who's going to move first. Are we going to see some of these sort of big capital equity investors, private equity funds, start to come in and say, hey, we're going to move in in a higher equity basis? Or are we going to see some banks say, hey, actually, we're going to be willing to back some of these recap-type strategies through lending?- Is this a potentially destabilizing event for the banking sector?KYLE CAMPBELL: I wouldn't think so.- I'm trying to compare it to what happened earlier this year.KYLE CAMPBELL: Right. Yeah. I mean, I think you're going to see some serious stress. And I wouldn't be surprised if at specific banks, you see some possible failures. I mean, you don't want to throw that term around too lightly. But yeah, it's possible that some banks could either have to be sold or go through some sort of an M&A activity to sort of right the ship here.I wouldn't expect it to get to a level where we're needing to see serious intervention by the government because they're sort of very well aware of what's going on in real time. But these things can snowball pretty quickly. So yeah, it could be something to watch for sure.- Yeah, most definitely. Kyle, thanks for coming in. Good to see you. Kyle Campbell, staff writer at American Banker, covering some various areas of risks for us.]

MOVES-Morgan Stanley hires Kagan from Citi for structured M&A -sources
column10: [By Anirban SenNEW YORK, July 24 (Reuters) - Morgan Stanley has hired Michael Kagan from Citigroup Inc to drive the bank's efforts on structured mergers and acquisitions (M&A), including spin-offs and separation deals, people familiar with the matter said on Monday.Kagan was Citigroup's North America head of shareholder advisory and structured solutions. The sources requested anonymity because the matter is confidential.Morgan Stanley and Citigroup declined to comment.Before joining Citi, Kagan worked on structuring deals at Goldman Sachs Group Inc for nearly a decade. He started his career as a tax associate at law firm Cleary Gottlieb Steen & Hamilton LLP.A number of Wall Street banks have investment banking teams that work on so-called structured deals, which include corporate restructuring transactions such as corporate carveouts and spin-outs.At Goldman Sachs, for instance, David Dubner leads its M&A structuring unit, while former Goldman banker Joe Todd spearheads Evercore Inc's spin-off business.Kagan's hiring comes as more companies mull ways to shed non-core assets amid concerns about an economic slowdown. Just in 2022, there were 30 separation deals globally, representing about 17% of all the spin-off transactions that were unveiled during the last decade, according to data compiled by Goldman Sachs and EY.Roughly half of such deals from the 2018-to-2022 period were worth over $5 billion, compared with a third from the 2012 to 2017 period that met that threshold, according to the Goldman-EY study.Morgan Stanley has also made other high-profile hires of late to boost its investment banking franchise. It hired Marco Caggiano, who previously served as JPMorgan Chase & Co's North America head of M&A, following the departure of veteran investment banker Rob Kindler, who is joining law firm Paul, Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton & Garrison LLP. (Reporting by Anirban Sen in New York Editing by Marguerita Choy)]

Earlier this month, it recruited Neil Wolitzer, a partner in real estate investment banking at Goldman, one of the sources said.Meanwhile, PJT Partners Inc, the boutique investment bank led by Paul Taubman, has hired Brendan Panda, a prominent aerospace & defense dealmaker, from Evercore, the sources said. Panda worked on several notable transactions during his time at Evercore, including Aerojet Rocketdyne's $4.7 billion sale to L3Harris.Panda will join PJT as a partner focused on the aerospace & defense sector, the sources said.Evercore, PJT Partners and Morgan Stanley declined to comment. column10: [Markets continue to trend higher, with the Dow Jones Industrial Average now on the longest win streak in history. The Nasdaq index is up 35% on the year, with the S&P 500 up nearly 20% since Jan. The upsurge is being driven by a number of growth stocks, many of which just reported strong second-quarter earnings. Yes, technology stocks have led the way thanks to artificial intelligence.Moving through the second half of this year, equities look to continue trending higher, lifted by a surge in growth stocks. Knowing which stocks to take a position in as the rally gathers steam will be important for investors. If you can only buy one growth stock, it better be one of these seven top growth stocks.Top Growth Stocks: Alphabet (GOOG, GOOGL)Hand of woman watering small plant in pot shaped like growing graph representing growth stocksSource: Khakimullin Aleksandr / ShutterstockAlphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL/NASDAQ:GOOG) just reported exceptionally strong second-quarter earnings. Driven largely by growth in its cloud-computing unit, Alphabet posted an EPS of $1.44, as compared to expectations for $1.34. Revenue came in at $74.6 billion, as compared to $72.82 billion. Better, its YouTube advertising revenue totaled $7.67 billion, as compared to expectations for $7.43 billion. Google Cloud’s revenue came in at $8.03 billion, as compared to a forecast for $7.87 billion. Other Bets, which include the Waymo self-driving car, reported a 48% increase in revenue to $285 million. These strong results show that Alphabet is back on track after last year’s downturn.InvestorPlace - Stock Market News, Stock Advice & Trading TipsWith the Q2 earnings bump, GOOGL stock has gained 46% this year, making it a top growth stock.Top Growth Stocks: American Airlines (AAL)A businessman holding a coin with a tree that grows and a tree that grows on a pile of money representing growth stocks. growth stocksSource: MEE KO DONG / ShutterstockTravel is back and airlines are flying high as a result. Chief among the carriers that are benefitting from rising travel demand is American Airlines (NASDAQ:AAL). The world’s largest international carrier just reported Q2 earnings that crushed Wall Street forecasts across the board. The company announced an EPS of $1.92 versus the $1.59 that was expected. Revenue came in at $14.06 billion compared to $13.74 billion which had been the consensus forecast on Wall Street.Story continuesThe airline also raised its forward guidance for all of this year, saying it now expects the current travel boom to continue throughout this year’s second half and into 2024. American Airlines’ strong Q2 print came after rival carrier United Airlines (NASDAQ:UAL) announced record earnings for the April through June period. With us now in the midst of the busy summer travel season, American Airlines can be expected to post even stronger Q3 results. Two, the stock is being weighed down by concerns about the actors and writers’ strike in Hollywood, which has shut down the production of TV shows and movies. However, the strike is likely to be temporary and Netflix is more immune than most studios to the strike’s impact.The main problem with Netflix’s Q2 print was the forward guidance. The company’s revenue in Q2 rose 2.7% from a year earlier to $8.19 billion, matching analysts’ expectations. EPS of $3.29 beat consensus forecasts for earnings of $2.86 a share. Most impressive, Netflix added 5.9 million net new subscribers during the quarter, which handily beat the 1.9 million that was expected. Netflix ended the quarter with 238.4 million paying subscribers worldwide.Unfortunately, Netflix called for revenue of $8.52 billion in the current third quarter, which was lower than the $8.67 billion that had been anticipated, sending the stock lower. column4: UPDATE 1-Evercore hires veteran investment banker Bergstein from Morgan Stanley -sources
column10: [(Updates with Evercore and PJT declining to comment in last paragraph)By David Carnevali and Mike StoneNEW YORK, July 26 (Reuters) - Evercore has hired veteran Morgan Stanley banker Seth Bergstein as a senior managing director to drive dealmaking in the global services sector, people familiar with the matter said on Wednesday.Bergstein, who served as head of Morgan Stanley's global services group for about two decades, held the title of vice chairman of investment banking prior to his departure from the bank.He started his career at the Wall Street bank in the late 1980s as a financial analyst and briefly joined Goldman Sachs in 1991 before returning to Morgan Stanley, according to his LinkedIn profile.Bergstein's exit is the latest in a flurry of executive moves from large banks to boutique firms and comes at a time of a slowdown in mergers and acquisitions (M&A) activity that has forced Wall Street's biggest banks to cut thousands of investment banking jobs.Global M&A volumes for the first half of 2023 fell 39% to $1.38 trillion, according to data from Dealogic.In recent months, Evercore has hired more than half a dozen senior bankers from bigger investment banking rivals such as Goldman Sachs to boost its coverage in sectors such as technology and industrials.In June, Evercore hired veteran technology banker Tammy Kiely and top aerospace & defense banker Michael Tarulli from Goldman. Earlier this month, it recruited Neil Wolitzer, a partner in real estate investment banking at Goldman, one of the sources said.Meanwhile, PJT Partners Inc, the boutique investment bank led by Paul Taubman, has hired Brendan Panda, a prominent aerospace & defense dealmaker, from Evercore, the sources said. Panda worked on several notable transactions during his time at Evercore, including Aerojet Rocketdyne's $4.7 billion sale to L3Harris.Panda will join PJT as a partner focused on the aerospace & defense sector, the sources said.Evercore, PJT Partners and Morgan Stanley declined to comment. (Reporting by David Carnevali in New York; Editing by Sonali Paul)]

column4: SPG Awarded Significant Contract to Provide Energy-Efficient CHP Solution for Union Beverage Packers
column10: [BROOKSHIRE, Texas, August 03, 2023--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Signal Power Group ("Signal Power" or "SPG") announced today that the company has been awarded a significant combined heat & power ("CHP") contract valued at over $10,000,000 with Union Beverage Packers, LLC ("UBP"). Under the terms of the agreement, Signal Power will procure, assemble, commission, and maintain the complete 3.5MW CHP system for a UBP facility in the state of New Jersey. This system will be powered by the SPG 4 turbine engine under Signal Power’s license with Honeywell International, Inc. The CHP system will deliver 3.5MW of carbon-reducing power generation fueled with natural gas and simultaneously will capture the heat from the turbine engine to produce steam required to meet UBP’s beverage plant needs. The system is expected to be commissioned and operational in mid-2024 and will be supported by a ten-year long-term service agreement provided by SPG to ensure a seamless solution."This is the first of many CHP solutions that we (SPG) expect to deploy over the next three years as our commercial and industrial customers look to transition from legacy diesel-fired equipment or grid-provided power to more efficient and cleaner distributed generation systems. Under the Biden administration’s Inflation Reduction Act, this type of power plant qualifies as green energy which is eligible for certain valuable tax credits and other financial advantages. Signal Power and its partner Honeywell are aligned on accelerating the transition to environmentally-friendly fuel sources, including renewable natural gas and hydrogen blended fuels that will provide our customers lower-cost alternatives and reduce their carbon footprint with a clean source of power," said Rob Marchitello, Chief Executive Officer of SPG."We are thrilled to introduce this revolutionary CHP solution that aligns with our vision of sustainability and environmental consciousness. By adopting this cutting-edge technology, we expect to not only significantly reduce our carbon footprint but also generate substantial cost savings. Thanks to the support and excellent information provided by the New Jersey Clean Energy Program, we are confident that our investment will pay off in as little as 24 months," said Yaron Gohar, CEO of UBP.Story continues"We are excited to see SPG's continued growth with its newest CHP project that utilizes the company’s differentiated turbine engine technology and leverages management expertise developed over decades. We look forward to continuing our support of Signal Power in this important work towards a more energy-efficient future," said John Moon, head of Morgan Stanley Energy Partners.SPG continues to serve its energy service, industrial and marine customers with a complete portfolio of solutions, including a patented controls technology and a proprietary multispeed gearbox delivering a range of speeds engineered for specific customer applications. SPG provides a wide range of service plans that include performance monitoring and predictive maintenance, further reducing downtime and costs.About SPGSPG is a leading provider of sustainable energy solutions, and related services for the global industrial, energy and marine markets. SPG’s product offerings include turbine drive trains and related solutions for electric power generation, including microgrids, datacenters, combined heat and power and mobile power solutions, natural resources applications and the marine end markets. SPG is a portfolio company of Morgan Stanley Energy Partners.About Morgan Stanley Energy PartnersMorgan Stanley Energy Partners, the energy-focused private equity business of Morgan Stanley Investment Management, is a leading energy private equity platform that makes privately negotiated equity and equity-related investments in energy companies located primarily in North America. column10: [BROOKSHIRE, Texas, August 03, 2023--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Signal Power Group ("Signal Power" or "SPG") announced today that the company has been awarded a significant combined heat & power ("CHP") contract valued at over $10,000,000 with Union Beverage Packers, LLC ("UBP"). Under the terms of the agreement, Signal Power will procure, assemble, commission, and maintain the complete 3.5MW CHP system for a UBP facility in the state of New Jersey. This system will be powered by the SPG 4 turbine engine under Signal Power’s license with Honeywell International, Inc. The CHP system will deliver 3.5MW of carbon-reducing power generation fueled with natural gas and simultaneously will capture the heat from the turbine engine to produce steam required to meet UBP’s beverage plant needs. The system is expected to be commissioned and operational in mid-2024 and will be supported by a ten-year long-term service agreement provided by SPG to ensure a seamless solution."This is the first of many CHP solutions that we (SPG) expect to deploy over the next three years as our commercial and industrial customers look to transition from legacy diesel-fired equipment or grid-provided power to more efficient and cleaner distributed generation systems. Under the Biden administration’s Inflation Reduction Act, this type of power plant qualifies as green energy which is eligible for certain valuable tax credits and other financial advantages. Signal Power and its partner Honeywell are aligned on accelerating the transition to environmentally-friendly fuel sources, including renewable natural gas and hydrogen blended fuels that will provide our customers lower-cost alternatives and reduce their carbon footprint with a clean source of power," said Rob Marchitello, Chief Executive Officer of SPG."We are thrilled to introduce this revolutionary CHP solution that aligns with our vision of sustainability and environmental consciousness. By adopting this cutting-edge technology, we expect to not only significantly reduce our carbon footprint but also generate substantial cost savings. Thanks to the support and excellent information provided by the New Jersey Clean Energy Program, we are confident that our investment will pay off in as little as 24 months," said Yaron Gohar, CEO of UBP.Story continues"We are excited to see SPG's continued growth with its newest CHP project that utilizes the company’s differentiated turbine engine technology and leverages management expertise developed over decades. We look forward to continuing our support of Signal Power in this important work towards a more energy-efficient future," said John Moon, head of Morgan Stanley Energy Partners.SPG continues to serve its energy service, industrial and marine customers with a complete portfolio of solutions, including a patented controls technology and a proprietary multispeed gearbox delivering a range of speeds engineered for specific customer applications. column4: Law Firm Dentons Splits From China Arm as Beijing Scrutiny Grows
column10: [(Bloomberg) -- Global law firm Dentons is splitting from its Chinese operations to comply with impending data regulations, one of the more significant withdrawals by a Western company as Beijing intensifies a campaign to curb leakages of valuable information.Most Read from BloombergRussia Calls Emergency Key Rate Meeting as Ruble PlungesHollywood Studios Offer Writers a New Deal With Push From Netflix, Iger to End StrikeTrump Indictment Lays Out Sweeping Georgia Election PlotRussia’s Emergency Rate Hike Fails to Lift Ruble After CrashChina Cuts Rate by Most Since 2020 as Economic Woes DeepenDentons, a law firm with partners from the US to Europe, is separating this month from its mainland arm in response to government mandates that tighten cybersecurity and data handling. Partner Beijing Dacheng Law Offices will gain full independence to serve domestic clients, Dentons said in a memo to clients.The global agency becomes the latest Western firm to resort to drastic measures to comply with sweeping restrictions on the handling and transfer of data within and beyond China that will take effect later this year. Among other things, Beijing’s new data security regime gives President Xi Jinping’s administration the power to shut down or fine companies that leak or mishandle sensitive information. Penalties include fines and suspensions.Xi’s administration has tightened control over the hoard of information produced by the nation’s companies, considered critical for steering the economy as well as future technologies such as AI. But the broad and vague nature of new regulations has spurred concerns about compliance, and the penalties for falling short. Morgan Stanley, for one, is shifting more than 200 technology developers — about a third of the tech cohort — out of mainland China after the country tightened access to troves of data stored onshore.Read more: Morgan Stanley Moves 200 Tech Experts From China on Data LawEvery business has been forced to weigh the costs of complying with cybersecurity and data security laws with the benefits of operating in the world’s No. 2 economy, said Tom Nunlist, a Shanghai-based associate director at Trivium China who focuses on tech policy.Story continues“The fact is that we will see more companies separate out their operations — maybe break partnerships — because of this,” he said. “The data security related regulations, data export security assessment stuff is extremely strict. Or at least it can be extremely strict. It’s been an absolute nightmare for everyone to deal with.”Financial institutions, automakers, electronics firms and consumer retailers are among the more active multinationals in the country. column10: [(Bloomberg) -- Global law firm Dentons is splitting from its Chinese operations to comply with impending data regulations, one of the more significant withdrawals by a Western company as Beijing intensifies a campaign to curb leakages of valuable information.Most Read from BloombergRussia Calls Emergency Key Rate Meeting as Ruble PlungesHollywood Studios Offer Writers a New Deal With Push From Netflix, Iger to End StrikeTrump Indictment Lays Out Sweeping Georgia Election PlotRussia’s Emergency Rate Hike Fails to Lift Ruble After CrashChina Cuts Rate by Most Since 2020 as Economic Woes DeepenDentons, a law firm with partners from the US to Europe, is separating this month from its mainland arm in response to government mandates that tighten cybersecurity and data handling. Partner Beijing Dacheng Law Offices will gain full independence to serve domestic clients, Dentons said in a memo to clients.The global agency becomes the latest Western firm to resort to drastic measures to comply with sweeping restrictions on the handling and transfer of data within and beyond China that will take effect later this year. Among other things, Beijing’s new data security regime gives President Xi Jinping’s administration the power to shut down or fine companies that leak or mishandle sensitive information. Penalties include fines and suspensions.Xi’s administration has tightened control over the hoard of information produced by the nation’s companies, considered critical for steering the economy as well as future technologies such as AI. But the broad and vague nature of new regulations has spurred concerns about compliance, and the penalties for falling short. Morgan Stanley, for one, is shifting more than 200 technology developers — about a third of the tech cohort — out of mainland China after the country tightened access to troves of data stored onshore.Read more: Morgan Stanley Moves 200 Tech Experts From China on Data LawEvery business has been forced to weigh the costs of complying with cybersecurity and data security laws with the benefits of operating in the world’s No. 2 economy, said Tom Nunlist, a Shanghai-based associate director at Trivium China who focuses on tech policy.Story continues“The fact is that we will see more companies separate out their operations — maybe break partnerships — because of this,” he said. “The data security related regulations, data export security assessment stuff is extremely strict. Or at least it can be extremely strict. It’s been an absolute nightmare for everyone to deal with.”Financial institutions, automakers, electronics firms and consumer retailers are among the more active multinationals in the country. Volkswagen AG, General Motors Co., Starbucks Corp., Intel Corp., Tesla Inc. and Apple Inc. are some of the largest household names with extensive Chinese operations.But banking in particular is considered one of the more sensitive sectors because of its integral economic role, and is party to valuable data on Chinese borrowers.Morgan Stanley’s remaining staff on the mainland have started to build a standalone China system to comply with local regulations. The new infrastructure, which may cost hundreds of millions of dollars, will be incompatible with its legacy global platforms as the lender overhauls its Asia strategy of handling client records.The twin moves coincide with Beijing’s growing willingness to go after foreign firms it accuses of violating local regulations. The government has imposed restrictions for instance on Micron Technology Inc., and regulators have this year launched investigations into consultancies such as Bain and Mintz.Read more: Data Rules Risk Making China ‘Digital Island,’ Companies SayDentons’s split was first reported by the Financial Times and specialist site Law.com. The law firm signed a deal in 2015 to link up with Dacheng Law Offices to create what was at the time the world’s largest legal firm. Among Dacheng’s clients were some of the largest state-owned enterprises, including PetroChina Co. and China Telecom Corp.Denton’s move was “in response to an evolving regulatory environment for Chinese law firms in China — including new mandates and requirements relating to data privacy, cybersecurity, capital control and governance,” the firm said in the memo.Dacheng will instead operate as a separate and independent legal entity under a “preferred firm” relationship with Dentons.“It will damage China’s links with the rest of the world in ways that might be difficult to perceive,” Nunlist said. “That really is going to be a cost of implementing the data security vision that China has laid out and frankly, I’m not sure that the Chinese government has fully reckoned with that reality.”--With assistance from Colum Murphy.(Updates with analyst’s commentary from the fourth paragraph)Most Read from Bloomberg BusinessweekPrivate Equity Firms Are Slow to Sell Holdings Amid Higher RatesOne Nassau County Has a Housing Crisis, the Other Nassau County Has a SolutionQuality Control Is a Secondhand Fashion Startup’s Key to Growth©2023 Bloomberg L.P.]

column10: [BROOKSHIRE, Texas, August 03, 2023--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Signal Power Group ("Signal Power" or "SPG") announced today that the company has been awarded a significant combined heat & power ("CHP") contract valued at over $10,000,000 with Union Beverage Packers, LLC ("UBP"). Under the terms of the agreement, Signal Power will procure, assemble, commission, and maintain the complete 3.5MW CHP system for a UBP facility in the state of New Jersey. This system will be powered by the SPG 4 turbine engine under Signal Power’s license with Honeywell International, Inc. The CHP system will deliver 3.5MW of carbon-reducing power generation fueled with natural gas and simultaneously will capture the heat from the turbine engine to produce steam required to meet UBP’s beverage plant needs. The system is expected to be commissioned and operational in mid-2024 and will be supported by a ten-year long-term service agreement provided by SPG to ensure a seamless solution."This is the first of many CHP solutions that we (SPG) expect to deploy over the next three years as our commercial and industrial customers look to transition from legacy diesel-fired equipment or grid-provided power to more efficient and cleaner distributed generation systems. Under the Biden administration’s Inflation Reduction Act, this type of power plant qualifies as green energy which is eligible for certain valuable tax credits and other financial advantages. Signal Power and its partner Honeywell are aligned on accelerating the transition to environmentally-friendly fuel sources, including renewable natural gas and hydrogen blended fuels that will provide our customers lower-cost alternatives and reduce their carbon footprint with a clean source of power," said Rob Marchitello, Chief Executive Officer of SPG."We are thrilled to introduce this revolutionary CHP solution that aligns with our vision of sustainability and environmental consciousness. By adopting this cutting-edge technology, we expect to not only significantly reduce our carbon footprint but also generate substantial cost savings. Thanks to the support and excellent information provided by the New Jersey Clean Energy Program, we are confident that our investment will pay off in as little as 24 months," said Yaron Gohar, CEO of UBP.Story continues"We are excited to see SPG's continued growth with its newest CHP project that utilizes the company’s differentiated turbine engine technology and leverages management expertise developed over decades. We look forward to continuing our support of Signal Power in this important work towards a more energy-efficient future," said John Moon, head of Morgan Stanley Energy Partners.SPG continues to serve its energy service, industrial and marine customers with a complete portfolio of solutions, including a patented controls technology and a proprietary multispeed gearbox delivering a range of speeds engineered for specific customer applications. SPG provides a wide range of service plans that include performance monitoring and predictive maintenance, further reducing downtime and costs.About SPGSPG is a leading provider of sustainable energy solutions, and related services for the global industrial, energy and marine markets. SPG’s product offerings include turbine drive trains and related solutions for electric power generation, including microgrids, datacenters, combined heat and power and mobile power solutions, natural resources applications and the marine end markets. SPG is a portfolio company of Morgan Stanley Energy Partners.About Morgan Stanley Energy PartnersMorgan Stanley Energy Partners, the energy-focused private equity business of Morgan Stanley Investment Management, is a leading energy private equity platform that makes privately negotiated equity and equity-related investments in energy companies located primarily in North America. Morgan Stanley Energy Partners pursues a differentiated investment strategy, focused on the buyout and build-up of strategically attractive, established energy businesses across the energy value chain in partnership with world-class management teams.
